title: TypeScript SDK: Dual-runtime Stream Facade for unified async-iterator + ReadableStream consumption
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background: Customers consume Redwood streaming responses in multiple environments (Node fetch streams, browser native ReadableStream, Deno/Cloudflare runtimes and the SDK's async iterator surfaces). Existing examples show how to convert between AsyncIterable and ReadableStream, but we continue to see friction: (1) inconsistent cancellation/backpressure semantics across runtimes, (2) fragile retry behavior when transient transport errors occur mid-stream, and (3) poor ergonomics for dual-consume scenarios (libraries that want an AsyncIterator while app code prefers a ReadableStream).

Goal: Implement a lightweight 'Stream Facade' in the TypeScript SDK that provides a single, well-documented primitive that: (a) exposes both an AsyncIterator and a ReadableStream surface (on demand), (b) preserves backpressure/cancellation semantics consistently across Node/Browser/Deno, (c) supports resumable reads via lightweight checkpoint tokens (optional), and (d) integrates retry and idempotency policies for recoverable transport failures. The facade is intended as a thin wrapper that composes with existing adapters (fetch response body, WebSocket frames, and internal framed RPC).

Proposed API sketch: 
- createStreamFacade(source, options) -> StreamFacade
- StreamFacade.asyncIterator(): AsyncIterable<MessageFrame>
- StreamFacade.readable(): ReadableStream<MessageFrame>
- StreamFacade.cancel(reason?): Promise<void>
- options: { checkpoint?: boolean, retryPolicy?: RetryPolicy, maxReplayWindowMs?: number, frameDecoder?: (bytes)=>MessageFrame }

Key behaviors: 
- Lazy materialization: The underlying transport is only consumed once regardless of how many surfaces are requested; calling asyncIterator() and readable() returns views over the same single-shared consumption pipeline. Consumers must be able to 'attach' to one surface or the other; second attachment is allowed but will forward the same frames (fan-out is supported via a small in-memory ring buffer with configurable size).
- Backpressure: For ReadableStream consumers we honor the underlying stream backpressure via the standard controller signals. For AsyncIterator consumers we provide a pull-based await next() promise that only resolves when a frame is available and respects cancellation. Both surfaces map to the same internal queue to ensure consistent timing semantics.
- Cancellation: cancel() triggers an immediate teardown and sends an idempotent cancellation token to the server when supported. Cancellation is propagated to both surfaces.
- Retry + Resume: If the transport dies mid-stream and the server supports lightweight resume (server returns a checkpoint token in metadata frames), the Stream Facade will automatically attempt to re-open the transport and request the remaining frames using the last checkpoint. The retry policy is pluggable and will surface progress events. If resume is not supported, the facade falls back to full-request retry (if idempotent) or surfaces an error.

Tradeoffs: 
- Complexity vs ergonomics: Providing both surfaces with consistent semantics requires an internal multiplexing layer. We choose a small bounded ring buffer to avoid unbounded memory usage at the cost of potential frame drops if consumers are extremely slow; in that case the facade will surface a clear 'consumer-lag' error and recommend increasing buffer size or switching to ReadableStream with chunked processing.
- Server support assumptions: The resume flow requires server-side checkpoint frames. We will default to conservative behavior when missing server support (do not attempt resume).

Implementation plan: 
1) Design and spec: finalize frame metadata shape and checkpoint headers (owner: Maya).
2) Core implementation: implement facade core + Node/browser adapters + TypeScript types (owner: Liam).
3) Retry/resume integration: implement pluggable RetryPolicy and checkpoint handshake (owner: Qing Park).
4) Examples & docs: migration guide showing AsyncIterator->ReadableStream, cancellation patterns, and a 'resumable streaming' demo (owner: Samir Patel).
5) Tests: unit tests for cross-surface timing, integration test with stub server that injects disconnects, and e2e with browser runner.
6) Rollout: behind 'ts-stream-facade' feature flag for 2 weeks, gather usage telemetry, then flip default on in ts-sdk-2.4.0.

Testing notes: Key scenarios to validate: dual-surface consumption, rapid attach/detach, cancellation race with in-flight frames, resume success/failure, consumer lag behavior under slow consumer, memory stress with ring buffer limits. Create fuzzer that reorders/resends frames to validate checkpoint correctness.

Observability: Emit structured debug events via the SDK diagnostics hook: 'stream.attached', 'stream.detached', 'stream.checkpoint', 'stream.retry.attempt', 'stream.retry.giveup', 'stream.cancelled'. Ensure these are lightweight and opt-out via config.

Acceptance criteria (for Done): 
- API surface implemented and typed with examples for both AsyncIterator and ReadableStream consumers.
- Unit + integration tests covering >90% of facade code paths.
- Migration doc + short example snippet added to SDK docs.
- Feature flag rollout completed with no regression alerts after 72 hours in canary.
comments: 2026-02-21: Kickoff meeting — agreed on facade direction and initial API sketch. PM prioritized after streaming ergonomics spike.
2026-02-27: Decided on bounded ring buffer size default=64 frames; added option to configure per-call. Action: add memory-pressure telemetry.
2026-03-03: Spike complete — Node adapters for native fetch and undici implemented. Observed small latency when attaching second surface (acceptable).
2026-03-08: Implemented basic resume handshake. Need to finalize server checkpoint header name and format (open PR in server repo).
2026-03-10: First review done. Security requested note about cancellation token MFA — follow-up to confirm tokens are short-lived and scoped (Qing).
